Zloczew Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Złoczew, Poland

Not demolished. Złoczew, granted town rights in 1605, saw Jewish settlement develop from the late 17th century, with a formal community by 1812; population reached 65% (1,501) by 1897, settling at 39% (2,067) by 1939. In September 1939, Germans killed about 200 people, including 142 Jews; roughly 1,400 were later transported via the Zduńska Wola and Łódź ghettos, while about 400 remaining residents formed a local ghetto before its August 1942 liquidation and deportation to Chełmno. This cemetery's founding date is disputed, though some sources place it as early as 1530, potentially making it one of the oldest preserved Jewish cemeteries in Poland. It holds the 142 victims of the 1939 massacre. German forces used matzevot to pave Błaszkowska Street during the war; postwar degradation continued, with only two 20th-century tombstones surviving - one damaged, the other (the Jachimek family's terrazzo stone) destroyed sometime between 2005-2011.
